evidence: @Entity({ name: 'user' }) on class UserEntity maps the class to a database table, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.
@PrimaryGeneratedColumn(), @Column({ type: String, unique: true, nullable: true }) and @Index() define the database schema and indexes, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.

@OneToOne(() => FileEntity, { eager: true }) @JoinColumn() and @ManyToOne(() => RoleEntity/StatusEntity, { eager: true }) set ORM relations and loading strategy, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.
@CreateDateColumn(), @UpdateDateColumn() and @DeleteDateColumn() configure ORM-managed timestamps and soft deletes, which is persistence (infrastructure) work.
UserEntity extends EntityRelationalHelper, a relational/ORM helper base class.
The file path is src/users/infrastructure/persistence/relational/entities/, and the file is used by user.repository.ts and user.mapper.ts, which shows it is a persistence model.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The layer model assigns this file to the domain layer because it matches the **/*.entity.ts pattern. In practice it is a TypeORM persistence model. It lives under infrastructure/persistence/relational, and its whole job is mapping to the database: table name, columns, indexes, relations, eager loading, join columns, and soft-delete and timestamp columns. That is persistence work, which belongs to the infrastructure layer, not the domain layer. The repository and mapper files in the same folder only treat it as a persistence type, and a separate domain model is mapped from it. The likely root cause is that the *.entity.ts pattern catches ORM entities. Even so, measured against its declared domain layer, the file holds a responsibility that belongs to infrastructure.
